questions.question: How do you structure your time in an LLD interview?

interviewer_intent.testing: Evaluating whether the candidate can manage time effectively under pressure and prioritize design activities in a structured manner
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers spend 30 minutes writing perfect code for one class instead of showing the overall design first, leaving no time to discuss trade-offs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Verbally announce your time allocation at the start: 'I'll spend 5 minutes clarifying, then 10 on the class structure' — shows metacognitive awareness

questions.direct_answer: A 45-minute LLD interview should follow this rough allocation: 5 minutes to clarify requirements and scope, 5 minutes to identify core entities and relationships, 10 minutes to sketch a class diagram on the whiteboard, 15 minutes to write key Java class skeletons with method signatures, and 10 minutes to discuss design patterns, trade-offs, and extensibility.

items: Clarify first: nail the requirements before drawing anything
Identify entities before drawing: think on paper, not at the diagram
Draw high-level first: boxes and relationships, then fill detail
Write code for the most interesting class, not all classes
Save time for design discussion: patterns, trade-offs, extensions
Verbalize throughout: the interviewer follows your design as you explain

answer_sections.content: Time management in LLD is critical — 45 minutes goes fast. I spend the first 5 minutes clarifying requirements: what are the key use cases, any specific constraints? Then 5 minutes identifying entities — I list the nouns and verbs on a corner of the board. Then 10 minutes on the class diagram: all classes, relationships, and key methods. For the remaining 25 minutes, I write Java class skeletons for the 2-3 most interesting or complex classes — not all of them — and discuss design patterns I'm applying. The biggest mistake is spending 30 minutes perfecting the class diagram before writing any code. Interviewers want to see code, not just boxes.

follow_up_questions: What if the interviewer asks you to code a specific method in detail?
How do you handle it if you realize mid-design that your initial approach was wrong?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot or ATM system
speakable_v2.hook: 45 minutes sounds like plenty for an LLD round — until you realize you spent 30 drawing boxes and ran out of time before writing a single line of Java.

beats.text: Time allocation is the most overlooked LLD skill. A structured split keeps you from over-investing in one phase and leaving interviewers without seeing your code.

groups.heading: Minutes 0 to 5 — Clarify
groups.text: Ask about key use cases and constraints before touching the board. This prevents designing the wrong thing.

groups.heading: Minutes 5 to 10 — Identify entities
groups.text: List the nouns and verbs in a corner. Don't draw yet — think first.

groups.heading: Minutes 10 to 20 — Class diagram
groups.text: Draw all classes, relationships, and key methods. High-level first, then fill in detail.

groups.heading: Minutes 20 to 35 — Java code
groups.text: Write class skeletons for the 2 or 3 most interesting classes. Not all of them — the interviewer wants depth over breadth.

groups.heading: Minutes 35 to 45 — Discuss
groups.text: Talk through design patterns, trade-offs, and how you'd extend for new requirements.

beats.text: candidates miss: spending 30 minutes perfecting the diagram and writing zero code. Interviewers need to see Java — not just boxes. Move to code before the diagram feels complete.

speakable_v2.cap: Clarify 5, entities 5, diagram 10, code 15, discuss 10. Verbalize throughout. The biggest mistake is a beautiful diagram with no code.

sections.title: Why Time Management Matters in LLD
sections.content: LLD interviews test your ability to **design a working system** under time pressure, not write production-ready code. The interviewer wants to see how you break down a vague problem ('design a parking lot') into classes, relationships, and behaviors. Most freshers fail because they dive into coding one class perfectly instead of showing the **big picture first**. Think of it like building a house: you need the blueprint before the detailed plumbing. A typical 45-minute LLD round has five distinct phases, each with a purpose. Spending too long on any one phase means you won't finish, and an incomplete design signals poor prioritization. The key insight: **breadth before depth**. Show the interviewer you can think systematically, then drill into details when asked. This mirrors real software design where you sketch the architecture before implementing every method.

sections.title: Annotating Your Whiteboard with Time Boxes
Key Points
content: **Phase 1 (5 min)**: Clarify functional requirements and explicitly state assumptions — write them on the whiteboard so the interviewer can course-correct early
**Phase 2 (5 min)**: Identify entities by listing nouns from the problem statement and determining relationships (composition, inheritance, associations)
**Phase 3 (10 min)**: Draw a class diagram with boxes for each class, showing inheritance hierarchies and key attributes — this is your design contract
**Phase 4 (15 min)**: Write Java class skeletons for 3-4 core classes with method signatures and brief comments — interviewers can fill in logic mentally
**Phase 5 (10 min)**: Discuss design patterns used, extensibility points, and trade-offs like thread safety or database schema — this shows senior thinking
**Breadth-first approach**: Show all classes before perfecting one — an incomplete but well-structured design beats one perfect class with no context
**Verbal checkpoints**: At 15 and 30 minutes, pause and say 'I'm moving to phase X now' — interviewers appreciate the structure and can redirect if needed

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: I'd structure a 45-minute LLD interview into five phases. First, I spend about 5 minutes clarifying requirements. I'd ask things like does the parking lot need to support motorcycles and trucks, or just cars? Do we charge hourly or have a flat rate? I write these assumptions in a corner of the whiteboard so the interviewer can correct me early if I'm off track. Next, another 5 minutes to identify entities. I list the nouns from the problem: parking lot, parking spot, vehicle, ticket, payment. I sketch rough boxes showing how they relate, like a parking lot has many spots. Then I spend 10 minutes drawing a proper class diagram. Each entity becomes a box with its key attributes and methods. I show inheritance where it makes sense, like Vehicle as a parent for Car and Motorcycle. I also mark enums like SpotType or VehicleType. The next 15 minutes go into writing Java class skeletons. I focus on the core classes like ParkingLot and the main operations: assign spot, release spot, calculate fee. I don't write full method bodies, just signatures with clear parameter names. Finally, the last 10 minutes are for discussion. I talk about design patterns I used, like Strategy for pricing or Singleton for the parking lot manager. I mention trade-offs, like how I'd handle concurrency if this were production. The biggest mistake freshers make is spending 30 minutes perfecting one class. Show breadth first. An incomplete but well-structured design is way better than one beautiful class with no context. I'd even say out loud at the start: I'm planning to spend 5 minutes on requirements, then 10 on the diagram. That shows I've got a plan and I'm not just winging it.

questions.question: What are the most common mistakes in LLD interviews and how do you avoid them?

interviewer_intent.testing: Assessing self-awareness about design pitfalls and whether the candidate has reflected on good LLD practices from study or mock interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers memorize design patterns but don't understand when NOT to use them, leading to over-engineered solutions for simple problems
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention a specific mistake you made in a past mock interview and how you corrected it — shows growth mindset and learning from experience

questions.direct_answer: Common LLD mistakes include jumping straight to coding without clarifying requirements, creating god classes that handle too many responsibilities violating SRP, forgetting to model enumerations for states and types, over-engineering with unnecessary patterns, and failing to articulate trade-offs. Avoid these by following a structured approach: clarify first, identify entities, model state machines, apply patterns only when justified, and always discuss alternatives.

items: No clarification: starting to design before fully understanding requirements
God class: ParkingLot that handles fees, tickets, display, everything
Missing enums: forgetting SpotType, VehicleType, OrderStatus
Wrong pattern: forcing a pattern where it doesn't fit naturally
No trade-off discussion: presenting design as perfect rather than discussing limitations
Only drawing, no code: interviewers want to see Java, not just boxes

answer_sections.content: The mistakes I've been most careful to avoid: jumping to design without requirements — I've seen people spend 20 minutes on a design and then realize they misunderstood the problem. Creating a god class that violates SRP — it's tempting to put everything in one class but SRP must be enforced. Forgetting state enumerations — SpotType, OrderStatus are central to the design and forgetting them makes the model incomplete. Forcing patterns — if I can't explain naturally why I'm using a pattern, I shouldn't use it. And only drawing diagrams without writing code — LLD interviews expect Java class skeletons with real method signatures, not just boxes.

How do you handle scope creep in an LLD interview?

speakable_v2.hook: LLD mistakes are predictable — and knowing them in advance means you can avoid them where other candidates stumble.

beats.text: Most LLD interview failures come from a small set of recurring mistakes. Knowing them ahead of time is half the battle.

items: Starting without clarifying: designing for 20 minutes then realizing you misunderstood the problem
God class: ParkingLot that calculates fees, issues tickets, and updates displays — SRP violation
Missing enums: forgetting SpotType, VehicleType, OrderStatus makes the model incomplete
Forcing patterns: if you can't explain why you're using a pattern, don't use it
Only drawing diagrams: interviewers want Java class skeletons with real method signatures — not just boxes

beats.text: A God class is the most common mistake. It's tempting to add fee calculation to ParkingLot because it's convenient. Resist it — the moment you ask 'what would make this class change?' and get three answers, it needs to be split.

non-obvious: not discussing trade-offs. Presenting your design as perfect is a red flag. Every design has trade-offs — saying 'I chose Strategy here for extensibility, but the cost is more classes' sounds more credible than saying it's the ideal solution.

speakable_v2.cap: Clarify first, split responsibilities, include enums, justify every pattern, and write code. Avoid these five and you're ahead of most candidates.

sections.title: Why LLD Interviews Trip Up Freshers
sections.content: LLD interviews feel deceptively simple because the problems sound familiar: design a parking lot, library system, or ATM. But freshers fail not because the domain is hard, but because they skip fundamental steps. The most common trap is **premature implementation** — you hear 'parking lot' and immediately start coding a ParkingLot class without clarifying whether it's a single-level garage or multi-story structure. Another killer is the **god class anti-pattern**: a ParkingLotManager that handles spot allocation, payment processing, vehicle tracking, and reporting. This violates the **Single Responsibility Principle** and makes the design impossible to extend. Freshers also forget that LLD isn't just about classes and methods — it's about **modeling state transitions**. A parking spot isn't just occupied or free; it might be reserved, under maintenance, or handicapped-only. Missing these enums and status flows shows surface-level thinking. The good news? These mistakes are predictable and avoidable with a structured approach.

sections.title: Before and After: Avoiding the God Class
Key Points
content: **Mistake 1: No requirements clarification** — freshers assume they know what 'parking lot' means and miss critical details like vehicle types, pricing models, or entrance/exit flows
**Mistake 2: God classes** — cramming all logic into one class violates SRP and makes testing impossible; split responsibilities into focused classes like SpotAllocator and PaymentProcessor
**Mistake 3: Missing enums and states** — forgetting to model SpotStatus, VehicleType, or PaymentStatus as enums leads to brittle string-based checks and magic values
**Mistake 4: Over-engineering** — applying Abstract Factory, Builder, and Strategy to a simple problem impresses no one; use patterns only when they solve a real extensibility need
**Mistake 5: No trade-off discussion** — freshers present one design as 'the answer' without acknowledging alternatives like using a HashMap vs PriorityQueue for spot assignment
**Mistake 6: Ignoring state transitions** — not showing how a ParkingSpot moves from AVAILABLE to OCCUPIED to RESERVED indicates shallow domain modeling
**Avoidance strategy**: Start every LLD with 'Let me clarify a few things' and end with 'Here's what I'd change if we needed X' — this frames your design as thoughtful, not dogmatic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The most common mistake I've seen, and honestly made myself in mock interviews, is jumping straight into code without clarifying requirements. You hear parking lot and think you know what it means, but the interviewer might be thinking multi-level garage with handicapped spots and electric vehicle charging, while you're coding a single-level lot for cars only. So I always start by asking: what vehicle types do we support? Is there reserved parking? How do we handle payment? The second big mistake is creating a god class. Freshers tend to make a ParkingLotManager that does everything: assigns spots, processes payments, generates reports, sends notifications. That violates the Single Responsibility Principle. Each of those should be its own class. I'd have a SpotAllocator for finding available spots, a PaymentProcessor for handling fees, and a ReportGenerator for stats. Another trap is forgetting enums. If you're checking spot status with strings like 'occupied' or 'free', that's a red flag. You need a SpotStatus enum with values like AVAILABLE, OCCUPIED, RESERVED, UNDER_MAINTENANCE. Same for vehicle types and payment methods. Over-engineering is also common. Freshers think they need to impress by using every design pattern they know. But if the problem is simple, keep the design simple. Don't use Abstract Factory for a parking lot unless the interviewer explicitly asks how you'd support multiple parking lot chains with different rules. Patterns should solve real extensibility problems, not be decorations. Finally, always discuss trade-offs. Don't present your design as the only option. Say something like: I used a HashMap for fast spot lookup, but if we needed to assign the closest spot to the entrance, I'd switch to a PriorityQueue ordered by distance. That shows you're thinking about alternatives, not just memorizing one solution. The key is structure: clarify, design broadly, code narrowly, and discuss trade-offs.

questions.question: How do you handle extended or follow-up requirements in an LLD interview?

interviewer_intent.testing: Checking whether the candidate designed for extensibility from the start and understands the Open-Closed Principle in practice, not just theory
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers modify existing classes directly, adding if-else checks for the new case, which violates OCP and shows the design wasn't flexible
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point to a specific abstraction you introduced earlier that now pays off: 'I used a SpotType enum so adding ELECTRIC_CHARGING is just one new value'

questions.direct_answer: When an interviewer adds a new requirement mid-design like 'now support electric vehicle charging', demonstrate extensibility by adding new classes or extending existing abstractions without modifying core logic. Apply the Open-Closed Principle: introduce a ChargingSpot subclass or a SpotCapability interface. If the design doesn't extend cleanly, acknowledge it honestly and explain what you'd refactor.

answer_sections.content: When an interviewer adds a follow-up requirement, I treat it as an OCP test. 'Now add electric vehicle charging spots' — I extend without modifying: add ElectricVehicle extends Vehicle, add CHARGING SpotType to the enum, add ChargingSpot extends ParkingSpot. None of the existing code changes. If the requirement truly requires changing existing classes, I acknowledge it: 'This would require modifying the FeeCalculator interface, which suggests my initial design should have used a more flexible approach from the start. Here's how I'd refactor it...' Showing that you can extend AND knowing when to refactor demonstrates design maturity. Never pretend your design handles everything perfectly from the start.

follow_up_questions: How do you extend the ATM design to support Bitcoin transactions?
What refactoring would you need if the library system needed to support e-books?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot or ATM system
speakable_v2.hook: When the interviewer adds a follow-up requirement mid-design, they're testing the Open/Closed Principle — and your ability to extend without panic.

beats.text: Follow-up requirements are a deliberate OCP test. The interviewer wants to see whether you can extend your design cleanly or whether you need to rewrite it.

items: Identify what's new: is it a new type, a new behavior, or a new flow?
Extend without modifying: add a new subclass, enum value, or strategy implementation
If modification is unavoidable, acknowledge it: say how you'd refactor and why your initial design could have been more flexible
Never pretend your design handles everything perfectly — that's a red flag

beats.text: Add EV charging spots: ElectricVehicle extends Vehicle, add CHARGING to SpotType enum, add ChargingSpot extends ParkingSpot. None of the existing code changes. That's OCP — and it's the answer the interviewer is looking for.

non-obvious: if the new requirement genuinely breaks your design, say so cleanly: 'This would require changing the FeeCalculator interface — my initial design should have used a more extensible approach. Here's how I'd refactor.' Showing you can recognize and articulate design debt is a strength, not a weakness.

speakable_v2.cap: Treat follow-ups as OCP tests. Extend with new classes first. If you must modify, acknowledge the trade-off and show the refactor. Never bluff.

What refactoring would you need for e-books in the library system?

sections.title: Why Interviewers Add Requirements Mid-Interview
sections.content: In almost every LLD interview, the interviewer will wait until you've sketched your initial design, then say something like: 'Great, now how would you add support for electric vehicle charging stations?' or 'What if we need reserved parking for VIPs?' This isn't a trick — it's a deliberate test of the **Open-Closed Principle**: software entities should be **open for extension but closed for modification**. The interviewer wants to see if your design uses **abstractions** like interfaces or abstract classes that let you add new behavior without changing existing code. If you have to go back and modify your ParkingSpot class by adding EV-specific fields, that's a red flag. A good design lets you introduce a new subclass or implementation without touching the original. Think of it like a power outlet: you can plug in new devices (extensions) without rewiring the house (modification). This also tests your **intellectual honesty**. Sometimes the new requirement genuinely breaks your design. A strong candidate says: 'My current design doesn't handle this cleanly. I'd need to refactor ParkingSpot into an interface with different implementations.' That's way better than hacking an if-else check into existing methods.

sections.title: Extending Design for Electric Vehicle Charging
Key Points
content: **Interviewers test OCP deliberately** — the mid-interview requirement change is a standard move to see if your design has proper abstraction layers for extension
**Extension via subclassing** — if you made ParkingSpot abstract or used an interface, you can add ChargingSpot as a new subclass without modifying existing spot types
**Extension via composition** — alternatively, use a SpotCapability interface that spots can implement for features like charging, valet service, or handicapped access
**Avoid modification red flags** — adding if-else checks in existing classes like 'if spot is EV then charge extra' shows you didn't design for flexibility
**Acknowledge refactoring needs** — if the new requirement genuinely breaks your design, say so: 'I'd need to introduce an interface here' — honesty beats hacking
**Enum extensibility** — if you used enums like SpotType, adding ELECTRIC_CHARGING is trivial; if you hardcoded strings, you're stuck modifying multiple places
**Discuss real-world context** — mention that in production, you'd weigh the cost of abstraction: 'If we only have one parking lot type, I might keep it simple until we need the second type'

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When the interviewer adds a new requirement like support for electric vehicle charging, my goal is to show that my design can extend without modifying existing classes. That's the Open-Closed Principle in action: open for extension, closed for modification. So first, I'd point to where I built in flexibility. If I made ParkingSpot an abstract class with a method like can accommodate vehicle, I'd say: I can introduce a new subclass called ChargingSpot that extends ParkingSpot. It overrides can accommodate to check if the vehicle is electric and has a compatible charging port. The core allocation logic in ParkingLotManager doesn't change at all. It still loops through spots and calls can accommodate. Now the list just includes ChargingSpot instances. Another approach is composition. Maybe I defined a SpotCapability interface with methods like requires special equipment. Then ChargingSpot implements that interface, and the allocation logic checks capabilities. Either way, I'm adding new types, not changing old code. The key is I don't go back and add if statements to my original StandardSpot class. That's a violation of OCP. If I find myself writing if spot type equals EV, that means my design wasn't flexible enough. Now, sometimes the new requirement genuinely doesn't fit the design. Maybe I didn't abstract ParkingSpot and made it a concrete class with hardcoded fields. In that case, I'd be honest: my current design doesn't extend cleanly here. I'd need to refactor ParkingSpot into an interface with multiple implementations. That's way better than pretending it works when it doesn't. Interviewers respect honesty. They're not expecting a perfect design on the first try. They want to see how you think through changes. I'd also mention that in production, I'd consider whether we really need the abstraction. If this is a one-time addition and we don't expect more spot types, keeping it simple might be fine. But if the business is planning five new spot types, I'd invest in the abstraction now. The main thing is showing I understand extensibility isn't just theory. It's about designing with seams where new behavior can plug in.

questions.question: What should you say when you're not sure about a design decision in an LLD interview?

interviewer_intent.testing: Evaluating intellectual honesty, decision-making under uncertainty, and whether the candidate treats design as collaborative dialogue rather than a solo performance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers either freeze when unsure or pretend certainty and bulldoze ahead with a questionable choice, both signaling poor judgment
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame your uncertainty as a question about priorities: 'This depends on whether we optimize for read speed or memory usage — which matters more here?' shows you're thinking in trade-offs

questions.direct_answer: When uncertain about a design decision, present both options with their trade-offs and either ask the interviewer's preference or make an explicit choice while acknowledging the alternative. Say something like: 'I could use a HashMap for O(1) spot lookup or a TreeMap for sorted iteration. For this interview, I'll use HashMap since fast lookup seems more critical, but in production I'd profile based on actual access patterns.'

answer_sections.content: When I face a design decision I'm unsure about, I present the trade-off explicitly. 'I'm considering two approaches: using an abstract Vehicle class which gives shared code but tighter inheritance coupling, versus an interface which is more flexible. For this parking lot, since the vehicles genuinely share attributes like licensePlate, I'll go with abstract class.' This shows design thinking even when uncertain. If I genuinely don't know, I say so: 'I'm not sure of the best pattern here — my instinct is Strategy, but I'm open to your guidance.' Interviewers often prefer a candidate who reasons through decisions honestly over one who makes confident-sounding choices without justification. Design is always about trade-offs, not perfect answers.

follow_up_questions: How do you communicate design uncertainty without seeming unprepared?
Is it better to make a decision and move on or discuss trade-offs extensively?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot or ATM system
speakable_v2.hook: Uncertainty in an LLD interview isn't a problem — pretending you're certain when you're not is.

beats.text: Every LLD has design decisions with no perfect answer. How you handle uncertainty tells the interviewer more about your maturity than the decision itself.

items: Name both options: 'I could use abstract class or interface here'
State the trade-off: 'abstract class gives shared code but limits multiple inheritance; interface is more flexible'
Make a decision with a reason: 'since vehicles genuinely share attributes, I'll use abstract class'
Invite guidance if genuinely unsure: 'my instinct is Strategy here, but I'm open to your perspective'

beats.text: Instead of saying 'I'll use a Strategy pattern' with no explanation, say: 'I'm using Strategy for FeeCalculator because pricing rules change independently of the parking flow — that's the reason, not just the pattern name.'

non-obvious: interviewers often prefer a candidate who reasons through a trade-off honestly over one who makes confident-sounding choices without justification. Design is always about trade-offs — presenting it that way is a sign of experience.

speakable_v2.cap: Name options, state trade-offs, make a decision, give the reason. If you're genuinely unsure, say so and invite guidance. Honest reasoning beats confident bluffing.

sections.title: Why Uncertainty Is Normal in LLD Interviews
sections.content: Here's a truth freshers don't hear enough: **uncertainty is expected** in LLD interviews. Design isn't math with one right answer. When you're deciding whether to use a HashMap or TreeMap for storing parking spots, or whether ParkingLot should be a Singleton, there are legitimate trade-offs. A strong candidate doesn't pretend to have instant certainty. Instead, they **make uncertainty visible** and turn it into a discussion. Think of the interviewer as a senior developer on your team, not a judge scoring you. When you say: 'I'm weighing two options here — HashMap for fast lookups or PriorityQueue for closest-spot assignment. Which is more important for this system?' you're showing **collaborative design thinking**. You're also testing whether the interviewer cares about that detail or wants you to move on. The worst move is freezing in silence. The second-worst is barreling ahead with a choice you're not confident in. The best move? **Verbalize the trade-off, pick one with a reason, and note the alternative**. This shows you can make decisions under uncertainty while staying intellectually honest — a critical skill for real software work where requirements are always incomplete.

sections.title: Verbalizing a Design Decision with Trade-Offs
Key Points
content: **Uncertainty is a signal to discuss** — when you're genuinely unsure, it often means the problem has legitimate design options that depend on unstated priorities
**Present both sides** — structure your uncertainty as 'Option A gives us X but costs Y, Option B gives us Z but costs W' — this shows you understand trade-offs
**Make a call and explain** — after presenting options, pick one and justify it: 'I'll go with HashMap for simplicity, but I'd revisit if we need sorted iteration'
**Ask clarifying questions** — turn uncertainty into collaboration: 'Does this parking lot prioritize fast exit or optimal space utilization?' helps narrow the design space
**Acknowledge production differences** — say 'For this interview I'll keep it simple with X, but in production I'd measure Y before choosing' — shows pragmatic thinking
**Never fake certainty** — if you're unsure whether Singleton is appropriate, don't confidently claim it is; discuss the pros (single instance) vs cons (testing difficulty)
**Silence is worse than discussion** — if you go quiet when stuck, the interviewer doesn't know if you're thinking or lost; verbalize 'I'm weighing two approaches here' keeps communication open

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I'm not sure about a design decision in an LLD interview, I don't pretend I have instant certainty. Design isn't math with one right answer. There are trade-offs everywhere. So I'd present both options I'm considering and explain what each gives us and what it costs. For example, let's say I'm deciding how to store parking spots. I might say: I'm weighing two approaches. I could use a HashMap with spot IDs as keys, which gives me O of 1 lookup when a customer exits and I need to find their spot by ticket ID. That's fast and simple. Or I could use a PriorityQueue ordered by distance from the entrance, which lets me always assign the closest available spot. That's better for customer experience but adds complexity and makes lookups slower. Then I'd either ask: which is more important for this system, fast exit processing or optimal spot assignment? That's a totally valid question. The interviewer might say don't worry about closest-spot logic, just get them a spot. Or they might say yeah, closest-first is a key feature. Now I know which way to go. If the interviewer doesn't give direction, I'd make a call and explain it: For this interview, I'll use HashMap because I think fast exit is more critical than closest-spot assignment. But I'd note the trade-off and say in production, I'd look at actual usage patterns. Maybe customers don't care about walking an extra 20 feet, so HashMap is fine. Or maybe closest-spot is a differentiator, so we'd invest in the PriorityQueue. The key is I'm not bulldozing ahead with a choice I'm unsure about, and I'm not freezing in silence. I'm making the uncertainty visible and turning it into a discussion. That's how real design works on a team. You don't have all the answers up front. You talk through options, weigh trade-offs, and make the best call with the info you have. I'd also avoid pretending something is definitely right when I'm guessing. If the interviewer asks should ParkingLot be a Singleton, and I'm not sure, I'd say: Singleton ensures one instance, which makes sense if there's truly one parking lot. But it makes testing harder because you can't easily mock it. I'd lean toward Singleton here, but I'd want to discuss whether we ever need multiple parking lots in the same system. That kind of honesty shows I'm thinking critically, not just reciting patterns.

questions.question: How do you demonstrate that you understand SOLID principles in an LLD interview?

interviewer_intent.testing: Assessing whether the candidate understands SOLID as practical design heuristics that emerge naturally, not just as acronyms to memorize and recite
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Freshers mention SOLID by name ('I'm using SRP here') without actually showing the problem it solves or the design smell it prevents
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a violation first, then fix it: 'This ParkingLotManager is doing too much, let me split out the payment logic' — teaching while designing

questions.direct_answer: Demonstrate SOLID by applying principles naturally during design, not as a checklist. Show SRP by splitting a god class into focused responsibilities. Show OCP by using interfaces so new vehicle types don't modify existing code. Show LSP by ensuring subclasses like Motorcycle can replace Vehicle without breaking logic. Show ISP with small interfaces like Payable instead of one giant IVehicle. Show DIP by depending on abstractions like PaymentProcessor interface, not concrete CreditCardProcessor.

items: SRP: 'I'm separating FeeCalculator because it has a different reason to change'
OCP: 'Adding a new vehicle type doesn't require changing ParkingLot — it extends Vehicle'
LSP: 'Car and Motorcycle both implement Vehicle correctly — they're interchangeable'
ISP: 'Separate Payable and Reservable interfaces — not everything can do both'
DIP: 'ParkingLot depends on IFeeCalculator, not HourlyFeeCalculator specifically'

answer_sections.content: The best way to demonstrate SOLID is to apply it naturally in your design narrative, not recite the acronym. When I create a FeeCalculator class, I say 'I'm putting the pricing logic here rather than in ParkingLot, because pricing has its own reason to change — that's SRP.' When I use an interface: 'I'm depending on FeeCalculator as an interface so ParkingLot doesn't need to know whether we're using hourly or daily pricing — that's DIP.' When I add ElectricVehicle: 'We can extend the vehicle hierarchy without modifying ParkingLot — that's OCP.' Weaving these principles into your design explanation shows fluency rather than recitation.

follow_up_questions: Can you give an example from your parking lot design where violating SOLID would cause a problem?
Which SOLID principle is most important to enforce first when time is limited?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot or ATM system
speakable_v2.hook: Knowing SOLID definitions is easy. Demonstrating SOLID fluency in a live design is what actually impresses interviewers.

beats.text: The best way to show SOLID is to weave it into your design narrative — not recite the acronym when asked. Apply each principle as you make each design decision.

groups.heading: SRP — say it while splitting classes
groups.text: 'I'm creating FeeCalculator as a separate class because pricing has its own reason to change — that's SRP.'

groups.heading: OCP — say it when adding abstractions
groups.text: 'Adding ElectricVehicle doesn't require changing ParkingLot — we extend without modifying. That's OCP.'

groups.heading: LSP — say it about subclasses
groups.text: 'Car and Motorcycle both implement Vehicle correctly — anywhere we use a Vehicle reference, either works. That's LSP.'

groups.heading: ISP — say it when creating interfaces
groups.text: 'I'm using separate Payable and Reservable interfaces — not everything can do both. That's ISP.'

groups.heading: DIP — say it about dependencies
groups.text: 'ParkingLot depends on FeeCalculator as an interface, not HourlyFeeCalculator specifically. That's DIP.'

beats.text: candidates miss: waiting for the interviewer to ask about SOLID. The fluent approach is to name each principle naturally as you apply it. That shows the principle guides your thinking — not just your recitation.

speakable_v2.cap: Don't recite SOLID — apply it and name it as you go. 'I'm doing this because of SRP' is worth ten times more than listing the acronym at the end.

sections.title: SOLID as Design Intuition, Not Checklist
sections.content: Freshers often treat **SOLID principles** like a checklist to mention in interviews: 'I used SRP here, OCP there, LSP over there.' But interviewers can tell when you're name-dropping versus actually applying the principles. The key is to **let SOLID emerge naturally** from your design decisions, not force it in. Think of SOLID as guardrails that keep your design clean, not decorations you add at the end. **Single Responsibility Principle** shows up when you notice a class doing too much and split it. **Open-Closed Principle** appears when you introduce interfaces so new features don't require modifying existing code. **Liskov Substitution Principle** comes into play when you ensure subclasses can truly replace their parent without breaking logic. **Interface Segregation Principle** matters when you avoid giant interfaces that force implementations to include unused methods. **Dependency Inversion Principle** kicks in when you depend on abstractions like PaymentProcessor, not concrete implementations like StripePaymentProcessor. The best way to demonstrate SOLID? **Show a problem, then solve it** using the principle. For example: 'This ParkingLotManager is handling spot allocation, payment, and reporting. That's three responsibilities. Let me split it into SpotAllocator, PaymentProcessor, and ReportGenerator.' You just applied SRP without saying the words.

sections.title: Applying SOLID Naturally in Parking Lot Design
Key Points
content: **SRP in action** — when you notice a class like ParkingLotManager handling allocation, payment, and notifications, split it into SpotAllocator, PaymentProcessor, NotificationService
**OCP in action** — when you use abstract Vehicle and introduce Motorcycle without changing ParkingLot code, you're applying OCP naturally
**LSP in action** — ensure HandicappedSpot can replace ParkingSpot in any context without breaking logic; don't throw exceptions in overridden methods that the base class returns normally
**ISP in action** — don't create a giant IVehicle interface with methods like refuel and charge and fly; split into Refuelable, Chargeable, Flyable so implementations only adopt what they need
**DIP in action** — ParkingLotManager depends on PaymentProcessor interface, not StripePaymentProcessor concrete class, so you can swap in PayPalProcessor without modifying manager code
**Show, don't tell** — instead of saying 'I'm using SRP', say 'This class is doing too much; let me extract the payment logic' — the principle emerges from the reasoning
**Violation first, fix second** — a powerful interview technique is to sketch a design with a violation (god class), acknowledge it, then refactor to show you recognize and correct design smells

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To demonstrate I understand SOLID principles in an LLD interview, I don't just mention the acronym. I apply the principles naturally while explaining my design decisions. Let me give you examples. For Single Responsibility Principle, I'd show it by splitting a god class. If I sketch a ParkingLotManager that's handling spot allocation, payment processing, and notification sending, I'd pause and say: This class is doing too much. Allocation is one responsibility, payment is another, and notifications are a third. Let me split this into SpotAllocator, PaymentProcessor, and NotificationService. Now each class has one reason to change. I didn't say SRP by name, but I applied it by recognizing the design smell. For Open-Closed Principle, I'd show it through extensibility. If I make Vehicle an abstract class with subclasses like Car and Motorcycle, I'd explain: When we add a new vehicle type like ElectricCar, we don't modify the existing allocation logic in ParkingLot. We just extend Vehicle. That's open for extension, closed for modification. The allocation code keeps calling vehicle dot get type, and ElectricCar provides its own implementation. For Liskov Substitution Principle, I'd check that subclasses are truly substitutable. If I have a HandicappedSpot that extends ParkingSpot, I'd make sure it doesn't break the contract. The base class method can accommodate returns a boolean. My subclass must also return a boolean, not throw an exception. If it did, you couldn't replace ParkingSpot with HandicappedSpot without breaking the caller. That's LSP. For Interface Segregation, I'd avoid giant interfaces. Instead of one IVehicle interface with methods like refuel, charge, and fly, I'd split it. Create a Refuelable interface for gas vehicles, a Chargeable interface for electric vehicles, and a Flyable interface for flying cars if we're doing a futuristic design. Then each vehicle implements only the interfaces it needs. A Motorcycle doesn't implement Flyable. That's ISP. For Dependency Inversion, I'd show it by depending on abstractions. If ParkingLotManager needs to process payments, I'd give it a PaymentProcessor interface, not a concrete StripePaymentProcessor class. That way, I can swap in a PayPalProcessor or a MockProcessor for testing without changing the manager code. High-level module depends on an abstraction, not a low-level implementation. That's DIP. The key is I'm not saying 'I'm applying SRP here' like it's a checkbox. I'm showing the problem, then showing how the principle fixes it. That's way more convincing. It shows I've internalized these as design heuristics, not just memorized an acronym. I also like to point out violations before fixing them. I might sketch a design with a god class, then say: Actually, this violates SRP. Let me refactor. That shows I can recognize design smells and know how to fix them, which is what you do in real code reviews.
